## Chapter 6: Pegs, Codes, and the Phonetic Trick

Try to remember a single number: _87_. Easy.

Try this one: _874,123,569,402_. Almost impossible without writing it down. Twelve digits exceeds working memory by several times. The digits have no internal structure, no semantic anchor, no rhythm. Each is interchangeable with any other. The string slides through the mind like water.

Now consider that the modern memory champion at international competition is asked to memorize _thousands_ of digits, in order, sometimes within five minutes of seeing them. They do this not because they have unusual brains — measured against ordinary people, their working memory and IQ are typically unremarkable — but because they have learned a specific old trick. They convert the digits into something the brain can hold.

The trick is called, in its most refined form, the **Major System** , and it is one of the most ingenious inventions in the long history of human attempts to remember things. Its core insight is that numbers, by themselves, are almost uniquely unfriendly to memory — abstract, structureless, semantically empty — but if you can transform numbers into _words_ , and words into _images_ , and images into vivid scenes that can be placed in a Memory Palace, you have converted the worst-case material of Chapter 4 into the best-case material of Chapter 5.

This chapter does four things. It explains why numbers are so hard for the human brain to hold — drawing on Stanislas Dehaene's account of _two_ number senses, and on what Chapter 4's framework predicts for material this disposable. It introduces the Major System and walks the reader through it carefully enough that they can start using it themselves on a six-digit string today. It briefly sketches two competing peg systems — the Dominic System and the Number-Shape System — to show how different practitioners have made different design choices. And it situates all of this within the second moment of Thread C: the dialogue between the mnemonic tradition and modern science. Where Chapter 5's dialogue was _the ancients intuited spatial encoding; modern science confirmed it_ , this chapter's dialogue is _the ancients invented phonetic transcoding; modern science explains why phonetic transcoding works on a brain that has two number systems, only one of which is symbol-bound_.

By the end of the chapter you will have a working tool for memorizing numbers — birthdays, phone numbers, codes, dates, and yes, thousands of digits of pi if you ever feel the urge — and a precise mechanistic account of why the tool works on the brain you actually have.

### 6.1 Why Numbers Are So Hard

Begin with the question. Why are numbers so much harder to hold than words? _Bread, eggs, broccoli, chicken, garlic_ — five items, easy. _5, 9, 3, 7, 4_ — five items, also five, also harder. The two lists have the same length. Both are arbitrary in their order. Why should the digit list be harder?

Several things are conspiring.

First, the digits are _semantically empty_. The number 7 has no meaning — no associations, no cousins, no context. _Bread_ has many: the smell, the texture, the act of buttering it, the bakery on the corner, the verbs you do to bread. When you encode _bread_ you are activating a rich semantic network, and that network helps the encoding stick. When you encode _7_ you are activating almost nothing — a numeral, a position in a counting sequence, possibly a quantity. The encoding has nowhere to go.

Second, the digits are _interchangeable_. The digit _7_ in _5,9,3,7,4_ is not distinguishable in any meaningful way from the digit _7_ in _5,9,7,3,4_. The position changes, but the digit itself does not. With words, even arbitrary ones, the mind can use slight associative differences (_broccoli_ is green, _chicken_ is alive, _garlic_ is sharp) to keep them separate. Digits offer no such anchors. Two strings that differ only in the order of digits look almost identical; the mind has nothing to grip.

Third, the digits are _structurally invariant_. The string _5,9,3,7,4_ has no rhythm, no rhyme, no pattern. It is a flat sequence of equally-weighted items. Words have stress, vowel patterns, consonant clusters; sentences have grammatical structure. Numbers, in their bare digit form, have only the linear order of the digits.

Fourth, and most fundamentally, _the human brain did not evolve to handle precise numbers_. This is a deep fact, and the rest of the chapter depends on it.

#### Two Number Senses

Stanislas Dehaene, in a body of work that has been one of the great syntheses of cognitive neuroscience, has argued that humans have not one but _two_ systems for thinking about quantity, and they are very different.

The first is what Dehaene calls the **approximate number sense** , sometimes labeled the "number sense" tout court. It is innate, present from infancy, present in many other animals (rats, pigeons, primates, fish). It allows us to estimate quantity _approximately_ : this jar has more beans than that one; this herd is larger than that one; this group is roughly twenty, not five and not a hundred. The approximate number sense does not handle precise values; it handles _ratios_ and _magnitudes_. A six-month-old infant can distinguish a display of eight dots from a display of sixteen, but cannot distinguish eight from nine. The approximate system gives a _fuzzy_ read of how much is there. It is fast, automatic, and works without language. It is, in the brain, broadly distributed but reliably involves a region in the parietal cortex called the intraparietal sulcus.

The second is what Dehaene calls the **exact number system** , and it is a different beast. It is not innate; it has to be learned, painfully, through years of education. It is _symbol-bound_ — it depends on the existence of words for numbers (_one, two, three_ in spoken language) and written numerals (_1, 2, 3_ in writing). Without the symbols, this system does not work. It allows us to represent precise quantities (_exactly seven_ , not _roughly seven_), to perform exact arithmetic, to manipulate quantities in language. This is the system that lets you know that 8 + 5 is exactly 13, not roughly 13. It is, in the brain, much more dependent on language regions and on the connections between language regions and the parietal regions where the approximate system lives.

The two systems coexist in any modern adult. When you are asked "is this group of dots more or less than that group?", the approximate system fires. When you are asked "what is the cube root of 64?", the exact system fires. When you are asked "what is _7_?", both fire — the approximate system gives you a felt sense of "a moderate number, less than ten, more than three," and the exact system gives you the symbol and its position in the counting sequence.

The crucial point for memory: the _exact_ number system is _symbol-bound_. It does not store quantities directly; it stores their symbolic labels. The string _5, 9, 3, 7, 4_ is, to this system, a string of arbitrary symbols — much like five letters of an alphabet you do not speak. There is no inner felt-quantity to grip, no rich semantic web to anchor the digits, only the symbols themselves and their order. And symbols, in isolation, are exactly the kind of material Chapter 4 said the brain disposes of most rapidly: meaningless, unstructured, without emotional tag.

This is why numbers are so hard. We can think about quantity (the approximate system) without thinking about exact numbers, and we can think about exact numbers (the exact system) only via symbols, and symbols-in-isolation are about as memorable as Ebbinghaus's nonsense syllables. _PEH JOX KEL_ and _5 9 3 7 4_ are, from the encoding system's point of view, very similar things.

The mnemonist's task is therefore clear: _transcode the numbers into something less symbolic and more semantic_. Specifically, transcode them into something the brain _does_ find easy to hold — vivid imagery, concrete objects, action — and let those images carry the digits into long-term storage on the back of the affordances we examined in Chapter 5.

#### Definition: Transcoding

**Transcoding** is the conversion of memory material from one representational format into another, more memorable format, before encoding. Mnemonic transcoding takes material the brain finds difficult (numbers, foreign vocabulary, arbitrary lists) and converts it into a format the brain finds easy (concrete imagery, semantic associations, spatial layouts). The mnemonist does not have a better memory than the non-mnemonist; the mnemonist has a better _pre-processing pipeline_ that delivers the same material to the encoding system in a more digestible form.

In plain language, this means: numbers go in, images come out, the images get remembered. The same memory machinery is doing the work, but it has been handed friendlier material. The Major System is the most refined and longest-practiced transcoding pipeline for converting digits into images.

### 6.2 The Major System: Phonetic Transcoding for Numbers

The Major System is most often attributed to a 17th-century German named Johann Winckelmann, refined by various later figures, but the core idea — assigning each digit to a consonant sound — is older and probably had multiple inventors. The system is not, ultimately, the work of any one person; it is a craft tradition, accumulated and stable for several centuries. Memory practitioners around the world use essentially the same scheme, with minor regional variations.

The system has three parts: a _digit-to-consonant code_ , a _word construction step_ , and an _image step_. Together they convert any string of digits into a sequence of vivid images that can be placed in a Memory Palace.

#### The Digit-to-Consonant Code

Each digit from 0 through 9 is assigned a consonant sound (not letter — the system is _phonetic_ , based on sounds). The conventional mapping in the most widespread English-language version is:

Digit | Consonant sounds | Mnemonic for the assignment  
---|---|---  
0 | s, z, soft c | _zero_ starts with z  
1 | t, d, th | each has one downstroke  
2 | n | n has two downstrokes  
3 | m | m has three downstrokes  
4 | r | _four_ ends in r  
5 | l | L is the Roman numeral for 50 (drop the zero)  
6 | sh, ch (soft), j, soft g | _six_ and _J_ have related strokes; or memorize visually  
7 | k, hard c, hard g, q | K can be drawn from two 7-shapes  
8 | f, v, ph | a script _f_ looks like a figure 8  
9 | p, b | _9_ mirrored looks like a _p_  
  
Pause and look at this carefully. The digit 0 corresponds to the _sound_ of _s_ , _z_ , or soft _c_ ; not to the _letter_. The digit 7 corresponds to the _sound_ of _k_ , hard _c_ , hard _g_ , or _q_. The digit 8 corresponds to the _sound_ of _f_ , _v_ , or _ph_. The system is _phonetic_ — it is about sounds, not letters — and the mapping is one-to-many: one digit maps to several consonant sounds that are phonetically similar (mostly, sounds produced in similar parts of the mouth).

Vowels (_a, e, i, o, u_) and the "weak" consonants (_w, h, y_) are ignored — they are _fillers_. They have no digit value; you can use them freely to construct words.

A consequence: any digit-string can be turned into a word (or a series of words) by reading off the consonant sounds, inserting vowels and fillers wherever you like to make pronounceable words.

#### The Word Construction Step

Take the digit string _34_. The corresponding consonants are _m_ (3) and _r_ (4). The string of consonant sounds: _m, r_. Now insert vowels to make a word: _m...r_ → _more_ , _mare_ , _Mary_ , _amour_ , _armor_ , _mire_ , _moor_. Many possibilities. Any of them encodes the digit pair _34_.

By convention, mnemonists settle on _one_ word per number (or per number-pair, or per number-triple) so that the same digit always cues the same word. This produces a personal _peg list_ — your private dictionary mapping each pair from 00 to 99 to a fixed word. Memorizing the peg list is the up-front investment; once it is done, any string of digits decomposes into chunks of two and is converted into known words instantly.

A standard 100-word peg list looks like this in sample (these are common choices, but each mnemonist tunes their own list to their own associations):

* _00_ : sauce (s-s)
* _01_ : seat (s-t)
* _02_ : sun (s-n)
* _03_ : sumo (s-m)
* _04_ : sore (s-r)
* _05_ : sail (s-l)
* _06_ : cash (s-sh)
* _07_ : sock (s-k)
* _08_ : safe (s-f)
* _09_ : soap (s-p)
* _10_ : toes (t-s)
* _11_ : tot (t-t)
* _12_ : tin (t-n)
* _13_ : tom (t-m)
* _14_ : tar (t-r)
* _15_ : tail (t-l)
* _16_ : dish (t-sh)
* _17_ : tack (t-k)
* _18_ : dove (t-v)
* _19_ : tube (t-b)
* _20_ : nose (n-s)
* _21_ : net (n-t)
* _22_ : nun (n-n)
* _23_ : name (n-m)
* _24_ : Nero (n-r)
* _25_ : nail (n-l)

…and so on, up to _99_. Each entry is a concrete noun — preferably one that produces a vivid image and can be visualized doing something. The full list takes some weeks to memorize fluently, but it is a one-time investment.

Some readers will notice immediately that this is more work than seems initially appealing. It is. But once the list is in place, it does astonishing things. To memorize a six-digit string like _314159_ , decompose into pairs (_31, 41, 59_), look up the words (_mat, rat, lip_), and construct a vivid scene combining them: _a rat sitting on a mat licking its lip_. Place that scene at the next location in your Memory Palace. You have just stored six digits as one image.

#### A Worked Example

Let us try to memorize the first ten digits of pi: _3.1415926535_.

Decompose into pairs: _31, 41, 59, 26, 53_ , plus the leading _3_ (or, more cleanly, treat as 3.14|15|92|65|35 if you prefer pairings starting after the decimal). Let us use _31, 41, 59, 26, 53_.

Look up the peg words: _mat (31), rat (41), lip (59), niche (26 — the pair n + sh gives words like _gnash_ , _niche_ , _nacho_ ; we use _niche_), lamb (53 — the pair l + m gives _lime_ , _loam_ , _lamb_ ; we use _lamb_)._

Take peg words: _mat, rat, lip, niche, lamb_.

Build a scene: imagine entering a new room of your palace. _On the mat, a rat is sitting, with an enormous prehensile lip. Behind the rat is an alcove or niche in the wall, in which a small lamb is curled up, asleep._ This is a slightly absurd composite image, but the absurdity is doing work (Chapter 7 will tell us why). Place it firmly at the next palace location.

You have just stored ten digits of pi (counting the leading 3) as one composite scene at one location. Multiply the procedure by ten locations and you have a hundred digits of pi.

This is the basic operation. With practice, the decomposition into pairs is automatic; the look-up of peg words is automatic; the scene-construction takes ten to thirty seconds per ten-digit string. Memory champions in international competitions are doing this at speed: hundreds of digits per minute, with a high success rate, sustained for the duration of the event.

#### Why It Works

Now we can name precisely why the Major System works on the brain we have.

_It converts symbol-bound material into semantic-bound material._ Digits are processed, as Section 6.1 argued, by the symbol-bound exact number system, which is anaemic and decay-prone. Words are processed by the rich semantic system, which is connected to vast networks of associations, imagery, and emotion. By forcing the digits to pass through a phonetic transformation into words, the mnemonist routes the material through the system that the brain holds well.

_It exploits phonological encoding._ The pairing of digit to consonant sound (not letter) leverages the brain's auditory phonological processing, which is among the most over-learned systems any literate adult has. You can recognize a sound and produce a word containing it without effort. This conversion is essentially free for a fluent speaker — much faster than trying to memorize digits directly.

_It produces concrete imagery._ The peg words are deliberately concrete nouns — _mat, rat, lip_ — which can be visualized vividly. Visualization engages the dual-coding apparatus we will meet in detail in Chapter 7: imagery plus verbal encoding produces stronger memory than either alone. The Major System is, by design, set up to feed the dual-coding system.

_It chunks digits into pairs._ Working memory holds about four chunks (Chapter 3); a string of fifty digits is fifty chunks for the unaided system but only twenty-five chunks (a still-too-many number, but reduced) when paired, and only a much smaller number of chunks when the pairs are bound into composite scenes at palace locations.

_It feeds into the Memory Palace._ The peg words can be placed at locations in a Memory Palace, exploiting the spatial-mapping system that we examined in Chapter 5. The system stacks: digits → consonants → words → images → spatial positions, with each transformation moving the material toward a more memorable format.

The whole thing is an elegant pipeline. Each step is a controlled transformation; each step delivers material in a slightly more memorable form to the next; and the final product is well within the brain's natural carrying capacity.

#### Common Misconception

A reader sometimes assumes that the Major System is, fundamentally, _just memorizing_ : instead of memorizing the digits, you memorize the peg words and the consonants and the rules, which is even more work. This is a partial truth that misses the deeper point.

It is true that the system requires up-front investment. Memorizing 100 peg words takes weeks of effort. But the up-front investment is _one-time_ , and once paid, it transforms the cost of memorizing any future digit string. Without the system, each new sequence of digits is fresh, expensive, and decay-prone. With the system, each new sequence is decomposed-and-imaged in a procedure that takes seconds and produces durable storage. The investment-vs-return is similar to learning to read: a multi-year painful acquisition that, once acquired, transforms the cost of every future encounter with text.

More deeply: the system is not "just memorizing harder." It is _converting an unfriendly format into a friendly one_ — the same brain machinery is doing the work, but it is now working on material it can hold rather than material it cannot. The Major System does not give you a better memory; it gives you a better _interface_ between the world's numerical demands and the memory you already have.

### 6.3 Other Peg Systems: The Design Space

The Major System is not the only mnemonic system for numbers. Several alternatives have been developed, each making different design choices and suited to different kinds of material or different mnemonist temperaments. Two are worth a brief look, both for the techniques themselves and for what their existence reveals about the design space.

#### The Dominic System

Dominic O'Brien, an English mnemonist who held the World Memory Championship multiple times in the 1990s, devised an alternative system that addresses what he saw as a limitation of the standard Major System: the peg words are _objects_ , but objects do not always lend themselves to vivid action.

In the Dominic System, each pair of digits maps not to an object but to a _person_ — typically a famous person whose initials match the digits when run through a slightly different code. The code is:

Digit | Letter  
---|---  
0 | O  
1 | A  
2 | B  
3 | C  
4 | D  
5 | E  
6 | S  
7 | G  
8 | H  
9 | N  
  
So the digits _07_ map to the letters O-G, which produce the initials of a person you choose: perhaps a friend named Owen Garcia, or — for those of a certain literary bent — Oscar Greene. Each pair is a person; each person comes with a characteristic action (their job, their habit, their famous gesture); and digits are encoded as scenes in which a particular person performs a particular action with a particular object.

For _31415926_ you would, in the Dominic System, encode _31_ (a person CA — for example, Carla Andrews), _41_ (DA — David Aboud), _59_ (EN — Eleanor Nash), _26_ (BS — Boris Smith). Now build a scene: _Carla Andrews bowing to David Aboud while Eleanor Nash and Boris Smith dance around them_. Each pair contributes a person performing some action.

Why might this be better than the Major System? O'Brien's argument: people are inherently more memorable than objects. Faces, personalities, characteristic actions — these engage emotional and social-cognitive systems that pure object imagery does not. The amygdala, the social-brain network, the face-recognition machinery — all these are now contributing to encoding alongside the spatial and semantic systems. The result, for O'Brien and many of his successors, was substantially faster encoding for very long digit strings under tournament conditions.

The trade-off: more up-front investment. You need a coherent set of 100 people whose initials you know, with characteristic actions, ready to be deployed at speed. This is a richer ontology than the Major System's word list and takes longer to acquire. For a casual mnemonist memorizing the occasional phone number, the Major System is simpler. For a tournament memorist memorizing thousands of digits, the Dominic System (or its further refinements, the Person-Action-Object systems used by current world champions) often wins.

#### The Number-Shape System

A third approach, sometimes called the _Number-Shape System_ , ignores phonetic codes entirely and instead maps each digit to an object whose _shape_ resembles the digit. This is a much simpler system, with a much shorter learning curve, and it works well for short digit strings even without prior training.

Digit | Shape Image  
---|---  
0 | Egg (or ring, or doughnut)  
1 | Pencil (or candle, or arrow)  
2 | Swan  
3 | Heart on its side (or handcuffs)  
4 | Sailboat  
5 | Hook  
6 | Cherry on its stem (or golf club)  
7 | Cliff edge  
8 | Snowman  
9 | Balloon on a string  
  
To remember the digits _7415_ , you build a scene: _a cliff (7) with a sailboat (4) below, on the deck of which a pencil (1) is balanced upright with a hook (5) hanging off it_. The scene is constructible without any training; anyone can do it. The trade-off: the system is much less efficient than the Major System or the Dominic System for long digit strings, because it processes one digit at a time rather than two.

The Number-Shape System is the system to recommend to a beginner who wants a small win quickly without paying the up-front cost of the more powerful systems. For a phone number, a PIN, a birthday, or a short access code, it works well. For competitive memorization, it is too slow.

#### What the Design Space Reveals

The existence of multiple peg systems — each making different design choices — tells us something important about mnemonic technique. There is no single right answer. The mnemonic problem (transcode numbers into rememberable form) admits multiple solutions, each of which trades off learning cost, encoding speed, retrieval reliability, and richness of imagery in different ways. The Major System emphasizes phonetic flexibility; the Dominic System emphasizes social-cognitive engagement; the Number-Shape System emphasizes immediate accessibility. All three work; all three are used; all three have their adherents.

This is, by analogy, the same situation programming languages occupy in software: there is no one best language, only a family of languages each making different design trade-offs, and the right language depends on what one is trying to do and what one is willing to pay in learning cost. Mnemonic systems are similarly a design space, not a single artifact, and the practitioner's choice depends on use case and preference.

#### Common Misconception

A common assumption is that memory champions are using a single canonical system that one could simply adopt off the shelf. The reality is that elite memorists often build _idiosyncratic_ systems — heavily customized blends of Major, Dominic, and other approaches, with personal peg lists tuned to their own associations, their own life, their own affective palette. A memory champion's peg list is often as personal as a writer's vocabulary or a musician's set of fingering preferences. Trying to copy a champion's system wholesale rarely works; the system relies on the champion's own associations, which are not transferable. The portable parts are the _principles_ (transcode unfriendly material into friendly material, exploit phonetic and imagistic encoding, build a personal system that you will own over years). The system itself, in its specific contents, is something each serious mnemonist constructs for themselves. We will return to this in Chapter 8 with a related point: the gap between what mnemonics can encode and what learning actually requires.

### 6.4 The Two-Way Interrogation, Continued

We come back to Thread C — the dialogue between the mnemonic tradition and the modern science of memory.

The mnemonic tradition arrived at the phonetic peg system without any explicit theory of why it should work. The early practitioners simply observed that _if you could turn numbers into words, the words stuck better_. This was an empirical discovery, refined over centuries, with no claim about underlying mechanism. Why words stuck better than numbers was not a question the tradition could answer.

The modern science offers an answer with cellular precision. The exact number system is symbol-bound and sparsely connected to other cognitive systems; the language and semantic systems are richly connected; the imagery and spatial systems are richly connected to both language and semantics. Forcing material to pass through phonetic-and-then-semantic encoding routes it through the brain's most richly connected machinery. Forcing it to pass through imagery routes it further into the same machinery. The peg system is, in the modern account, a precisely targeted exploitation of the brain's actual representational topology — the digits are dragged out of their isolated number-system island and into the mainland of richly-connected language-and-imagery cognition.

This is a second moment of _vindication_ for the mnemonic tradition. The practitioners did not know about the dual number sense. They did not know about the parietal locus of the approximate number system or its sparse connection to the rest of cognition. They did not know that "phonetic" was a meaningful neural category corresponding to specific brain pathways. They knew that the trick worked, and they refined the trick across centuries. Modern science has named what the trick was doing.

But this dialogue is also the first place we can begin to feel the limits of what the mnemonic tradition saw. The peg system is a brilliant _encoding_ technology. It takes input that the brain cannot hold and converts it into input that the brain can hold. What it does not do — and what Chapter 9 will press hard on — is _strengthen the trace through the right kind of practice_. Once the digits have been encoded as a vivid scene at a palace location, the scene is laid down; from that point onward, the question of whether the scene survives depends on consolidation, on retrieval practice, on spacing. The mnemonic tradition's tools ended at the encoding. The science of the next several chapters will reveal what comes after.

For now, Thread C records: phonetic transcoding, intuited by the practitioners; mechanism named by Dehaene's account of the dual number system; another moment of mutual confirmation in the conversation that defines the book.

### 6.5 What This Chapter Has Done

We have introduced the second great pillar of the mnemonic tradition: the systematic conversion of digits into images via phonetic transcoding. We have walked through the Major System in enough detail that the reader can begin using it on six-digit strings today. We have placed the system in its design-space context, with the Dominic System and the Number-Shape System as alternative architectures making different trade-offs. And we have continued the two-way interrogation with modern memory science: the practitioners discovered phonetic transcoding by introspection and refinement; Dehaene and others have articulated why phonetic transcoding works on the human brain — because numbers are processed by a sparse, symbol-bound exact system, and routing them through phonetic-and-imagery channels engages systems with vastly richer connectivity.

The chapter has also continued the meta-pedagogical thread of Thread B: the embedded practice for this chapter is to take the _first three digits_ of your own phone number and, using the Major System (or the Number-Shape System if you prefer), encode them as a vivid scene at the next location of your Memory Palace. Try it now. Do not over-think it. If your phone number begins with _312_ , decompose into _31, 2_ — consult the peg list above, find _mat_ and _no_ (n with a vowel, since 2 = n; _no_ or _Noah_) — and build a quick scene: _a mat with the word "no" written on it in big red letters; or a mat on which Noah's ark sits, animals two-by-two boarding it_. Place at the next location. Walk on.

Where we go from here. Chapter 7 takes a closer look at _why some images stick and others slide off_ — the question of distinctiveness, dual coding, and emotional tagging. The mnemonic tradition has long advised practitioners to make their images _bizarre, violent, sexual, or otherwise emotionally charged_. The reasons (von Restorff effect, amygdala-mediated tagging, Paivio's dual-coding theory) reveal that the practitioners were exploiting a deeper feature of memory — and reveal, as a darker corollary, why hate ads, conspiracy imagery, and shock political content work disproportionately well, since they tap the same affordances. Chapter 8 will then be the honest chapter where we ask where the bag of tricks runs out, and Chapter 9 will be the turn where the science forces us to admit that even the encoding lever was not the right lever.

For now: the digits, transcoded; the system, sketched; the dialogue, advanced.

### 6.6 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** In your own words, explain why numbers (e.g., a string of ten digits) are uniquely difficult for human memory to hold compared to a string of ten common words. What does Stanislas Dehaene's account of _two number senses_ contribute to this explanation?

Hint

The chapter argued that the exact number system is symbol-bound, while the approximate number system handles only fuzzy magnitudes, and that semantic networks for words are vastly richer than for digits.

**Answer:** Numbers are uniquely difficult because the human brain has no system that handles precise digit strings naturally. Dehaene's account distinguishes two number senses: an _approximate number sense_ , innate, fast, automatic, present in infants and many animals, that handles fuzzy magnitudes ("more, fewer, roughly twenty"); and an _exact number system_ , learned through education, symbol-bound, that handles precise quantities only via the linguistic and numerical symbols a culture provides. The exact system is the one engaged by a digit string like _5,9,3,7,4_. It is symbol-bound — meaning the system stores the symbols themselves, not any inner felt-quantity — and the symbols are sparsely connected to the rest of cognition. By contrast, common words are handled by the rich semantic network: each word activates associations, imagery, sound patterns, contextual memories, and emotional responses that anchor the word in many ways. _Bread_ is connected to thousands of other things; _7_ is connected to almost nothing besides its position in a counting sequence and the symbol itself. Furthermore, digits are interchangeable (one _7_ looks like any other _7_), structurally invariant (no rhythm or pattern within a string), and emotionally neutral (a digit string evokes no feeling). All of these put a digit string very near the worst-case end of Chapter 4's forgetting curve. Words, with their semantic richness, sit much further toward the best-case end. The two number senses explain the underlying reason: the brain handles approximate quantity well because it evolved to, and handles exact quantity poorly because exact quantity requires symbols, which the brain processes in a system that lacks the connective richness of semantic and imagistic processing.

**Q2.** What is _phonetic transcoding_ in the context of the Major System, and why does it produce more memorable material than the original digit string?

**Answer:** Phonetic transcoding is the systematic conversion of digits into consonant _sounds_ (not letters) — for example, in the Major System, 1 → _t/d_ , 2 → _n_ , 3 → _m_ , 4 → _r_ , and so on. Once the consonants are obtained, vowels and weak consonants (_w, h, y_) can be inserted to construct pronounceable words: the digit pair _31_ becomes the consonant pair _m-t_ , which produces words like _mat_ , _meat_ , _mate_ , _moat_. Each digit pair from 00 to 99 is conventionally bound to a specific concrete-noun word in the mnemonist's personal peg list, so any digit string can be decomposed into pairs and converted into a sequence of known words instantly. Phonetic transcoding produces more memorable material because it routes the digits out of the symbol-bound exact number system and into the rich phonological and semantic systems: the resulting words are concrete nouns (typically), can be visualized vividly, can be combined into action-bearing scenes, and can be placed at locations in a Memory Palace. The same brain machinery is doing the encoding; what has changed is the format of the input. Words are far more memorable than digits because the systems that process words are richly connected to imagery, semantics, and (via spatial encoding) episodic memory, whereas the system that processes digits is sparse and isolated. The Major System is a pre-processing pipeline that hands the encoding system better-formed material.

**Q3.** Compare and contrast the Major System and the Dominic System. What design choice does each make, and why might a practitioner choose one over the other?

**Answer:** Both systems are pegging systems that bind each pair of digits to a memorable element used to construct vivid scenes. They differ in _what_ the element is. The _Major System_ binds each pair of digits to a _concrete object word_ , derived through phonetic transcoding (digit pair → consonant pair → word). The _Dominic System_ binds each pair of digits to a _person_ , derived through a digit-to-letter code (with each pair giving the initials of a chosen person). In the Major System, encoding produces scenes of objects in action ("a mat with a rat on it"); in the Dominic System, encoding produces scenes of people performing characteristic actions ("Carla Andrews bowing to David Aboud"). The design rationale for the Dominic System is that _people are inherently more memorable than objects_ : faces, personalities, characteristic gestures, social-cognitive engagement — all of these recruit additional memory machinery (the face-recognition system, the social brain network, emotional engagement with persons) that pure object imagery does not. Practitioners working with very long digit strings under speed conditions — competitive memorists especially — often prefer the Dominic System (or its further refinements) because the encoding is faster and the imagery richer. The trade-off is more up-front investment: the practitioner needs a coherent set of 100 people with characteristic actions, fluent at speed, which is a more demanding ontology to build than a 100-word object list. A casual mnemonist memorizing the occasional phone number is usually better served by the simpler Major System; an aspiring memory champion may invest in the Dominic System (or build their own further refinement); and a beginner who wants quick wins can start with the even simpler Number-Shape System (where each digit is one shape-image) and migrate to the more powerful systems as their commitment grows.

**Q4.** Connecting back to Chapter 4: why does the up-front investment of memorizing a 100-word peg list pay off, given the chapter's argument about the rapid decay of unstructured material?

Hint

What kind of material is the peg list itself? Is it the disposable end of the spectrum, or does the peg list have features (semantic richness, structure, repeated use) that put it at the best-case end?

**Answer:** The investment pays off because the peg list, once acquired, is _not_ unstructured material at the disposable end of Chapter 4's forgetting curve. The peg list has nearly every feature that puts material at the best-case end. _Semantic anchor:_ each peg word is a concrete noun with rich semantic associations (a mat, a rat, a tin). _Structure:_ the list is bound to a clean phonetic code, so each entry sits in a known position in a system rather than floating loose. _Use:_ the peg list is engaged whenever the mnemonist memorizes any digit string, which means hundreds or thousands of retrievals over the lifetime of practice — and as we will see formally in Chapter 9, retrieval practice is the most powerful consolidation mechanism. _Connection:_ each peg word is linked to many subsequent digit-encoding scenes, building a vast associative web. _Emotional engagement:_ the practitioner cares about the list (it is the foundation of their memory work) and engages with it actively rather than passively. All of these features push the peg list to a forgetting curve that is essentially flat over decades. The up-front investment of memorizing the list is real (some weeks of work) but is amortized over years or decades of accelerated digit-memorization, with the list itself being so well-consolidated that it is essentially permanent. By contrast, every digit string you fail to encode in this way will follow Ebbinghaus's worst-case curve and will be lost. The Major System is, in effect, a _trade_ : pay an up-front cost to build a stable peg list with best-case retention properties, and receive the ability to convert all future digit strings into best-case-retention scenes for the rest of your life. The economics are excellent for anyone who memorizes digits regularly.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Using the Major System digit-to-consonant code introduced in Section 6.2, encode each of the following digit pairs as a word. (Choose any reasonable word that uses only the listed consonant sounds, with vowels and weak consonants — _w, h, y_ — as fillers.) Then construct a vivid scene combining all four words and describe where you would place it in your Memory Palace.

a) _32_  
b) _17_  
c) _50_  
d) _96_

Hint

3 → m, 2 → n, so _32_ maps to consonants m-n. Possible words: _mine_ , _moon_ , _man_. 1 → t/d, 7 → k/hard c/g. Possible words: _tack_ , _deck_ , _dog_. 5 → l, 0 → s/z. Possible words: _lace_ , _lass_ , _louse_. 9 → p/b, 6 → sh/ch/j. Possible words: _bush_ , _push_ , _pouch_.

**Answer:** Sample answer — readers' specific choices may vary, but the underlying decompositions should match.

a) _32_ (m-n): possible words include _moon_ , _mine_ , _man_ , _menu_. Choose _moon_.

b) _17_ (t-k or d-k): possible words include _tack_ , _deck_ , _duck_ , _dog_. Choose _duck_.

c) _50_ (l-s or l-z): possible words include _lace_ , _lass_ , _louse_ , _lasso_. Choose _lasso_.

d) _96_ (p-sh or b-sh or b-ch): possible words include _bush_ , _push_ , _pouch_ , _peach_. Choose _bush_.

Construct a scene combining the four words: _the moon has come down to earth and is sitting on the lawn; a duck waddles up and quacks at it; a lasso flies down from above and ropes the moon at its waist; a bush grows up rapidly behind, surrounding the whole tableau and lifting it gently into the air_.

Place this scene in your Memory Palace at, say, the _study_ (the room at the location after the dining room in the path established in Chapter 5). When you walk into the study, the scene is there; the four words are recoverable as _moon, duck, lasso, bush_ ; the digit pairs are recoverable as _32, 17, 50, 96_. Eight digits stored as one image at one location.

(The choice of words is somewhat personal — pick what produces the most vivid imagery for you, while staying inside the consonant rules. Once you have decided your peg word for _32_ , _17_ , _50_ , _96_ , etc., commit to those choices for future use, so that the pairing becomes automatic.)

**Q2.** Take a phone number, PIN, or birthday from your own life that you would like to memorize more reliably. Choose the technique you find most appealing (Major System, Dominic System, or Number-Shape System) and walk through, in writing, exactly how you would encode it as a scene at a location in your Memory Palace. Be specific. After encoding, comment on which features of the chosen technique made the encoding feel easy or difficult.

Hint

The reader's own answer will vary. Below is one worked example using the Number-Shape System for a sample seven-digit string, intended as a model.

**Answer:** A worked example. Suppose the digit string is _3145926_.

_Choice of technique:_ the Number-Shape System, because the reader has not yet built a Major System peg list and wants a quick win.

_Number-shape mappings used (from Section 6.3):_ 3 = heart on its side; 1 = pencil; 4 = sailboat; 5 = hook; 9 = balloon on a string; 2 = swan; 6 = cherry on its stem.

_Construct a scene combining the seven shapes in order_ : imagine entering the next room of your palace (say, the _library_). In the centre of the room is _a heart_ (3) lying on its side on a low table. Sticking out of the heart is _a pencil_ (1) writing words on the air. Beside the table is _a sailboat_ (4) on which a small _hook_ (5) hangs from the mast. Tied to the hook is _a balloon_ (9), drifting up. Out of the balloon hatches a _swan_ (2), surprising. The swan, in turn, has a _cherry_ (6) in its beak, with the stem trailing.

To retrieve the digits, walk into the library, see the scene, and read off the shapes in order: heart, pencil, sailboat, hook, balloon, swan, cherry → 3, 1, 4, 5, 9, 2, 6.

_Reflection on what felt easy or difficult:_ The Number-Shape System is appealing because it requires almost no prior training — anyone can use it immediately. The encoding produced a vivid scene in a few minutes. The challenge was _combining_ seven shapes into a single coherent scene; with this many items, the scene becomes either crowded or incoherent. The Major System would have compressed seven digits into about three or four words (e.g., _314_ = some word, _59_ = _lip_ , _26_ = _niche_) and produced a tighter scene. The Number-Shape System is excellent for short strings (3–5 digits) and starts to feel cumbersome at 6+ digits, which is why memory athletes graduate to the Major or Dominic systems for longer material. For a seven-digit phone number, the Number-Shape System works but is at its upper limit of practical use; for the 16-digit credit card number, it would be impractical and a phonetic peg system would be needed.

**Q3.** Connecting back to Chapters 3 and 5: when you encode a digit string using the Major System, several memory systems and brain structures are engaged in coordination. Identify the key systems and structures involved at each step (digit → consonant → word → image → palace location), and briefly explain what each contributes.

Hint

The phonetic transcoding step engages language and phonological processing. The word-construction step engages semantic memory. The imagery step engages visual imagery and the dual-coding apparatus. The palace placement engages spatial-and-episodic machinery (Chapter 5's hippocampal account).

**Answer:** Walking through the Major System pipeline, the engaged systems are:

_Step 1 — digits read in._ The exact number system is engaged momentarily as the digits are perceived. This system is parietal (around the intraparietal sulcus) and sparsely connected. If we stopped here, we would be at the worst-case end of Chapter 4's curve.

_Step 2 — phonetic transcoding (digit → consonant sound)._ The phonological-processing system is engaged: the regions of cortex that handle speech sounds (largely temporal and inferior frontal areas) take over the representation. This is a much richer system than the exact number system, with vastly more connections to the rest of cognition. The digits are now represented as sound patterns, not as numerals.

_Step 3 — word construction (consonant sounds → words)._ The semantic system is engaged: vowels are inserted, the consonant pattern becomes a recognizable word, and the word activates its semantic network (the _mat_ word activates associations with _floor_ , _door_ , _wipe your feet_ , etc.). This is a major step up in connectivity: the word is now embedded in a vast network of meanings and associations.

_Step 4 — imagery (word → vivid scene)._ The visual imagery system is engaged: the word _mat_ triggers a mental image of a particular mat, the word _rat_ triggers a particular rat, and the combined scene is constructed in visual imagery. This recruits the visual cortex (in a top-down, imagery-generating mode), the dual-coding apparatus (visual + verbal — Paivio's framework, which we will meet in Chapter 7), and frequently the emotional-tagging system (the amygdala) if the imagery is bizarre or vivid enough to trigger it. The material is now in the strongest format the brain has for retention.

_Step 5 — palace placement (scene → location)._ The spatial-mapping system (the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, with place cells and grid cells, as discussed in Chapter 5) is engaged: the scene is anchored to a specific position in a familiar imagined space. The hippocampus's binding function fuses the scene's features into a unified retrievable trace, and the spatial layout provides the retrieval cue at recall time.

_Steps 1–5, in summary:_ the digits enter through the sparsest, most decay-prone system the brain has (the exact number system), and they exit, after four transformations, into the richest, most retention-friendly system the brain has (a hippocampally-bound spatial-episodic trace with full visual imagery). Working memory has been used as the workspace at every step, but the heavy lifting is done by the chain of transformations. Procedural memory has been quietly involved as well: the Major System practitioner has, with practice, automated each transformation, so that the entire pipeline runs in seconds without conscious effort. The Major System is, viewed mechanistically, an elegantly engineered pipeline that routes material through every memory-friendly system the brain has, in series, before depositing it for storage.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The Major System and the Dominic System both convert digits into vivid imagery, but they differ in the _kind_ of imagery they generate (objects vs. people). The chapter mentioned in passing that elite memorists often build idiosyncratic systems combining several approaches and tuned to their own lives and associations. What does this tell us about the relationship between mnemonic systems and the mnemonist's individual cognition? Is mnemonic technique a portable, universal craft, or is it inherently personal?

**Discussion:** This is a deep question and the honest answer is "both, in different layers."

The _principles_ of mnemonic technique are portable and universal. The insights — that unfriendly material should be transcoded into friendly material, that imagery is more memorable than abstraction, that spatial layouts make excellent retrieval scaffolds, that distinctive and emotionally charged imagery sticks more than bland imagery — generalize across mnemonists, across cultures, and (so far as we can tell) across millennia. The principles describe what the brain does well and what it does poorly, and the brain's preferences are roughly the same across people.

The _implementations_ of mnemonic technique, however, are deeply personal. The Major System provides a phonetic code, but the _peg word_ you choose for _31_ depends on what concrete noun beginning with _m-t_ is most vivid to you. _Mat_ , _meat_ , _mate_ , _moat_ , _meadow_ — different mnemonists settle on different choices, often without fully knowing why, and once settled, the choice becomes part of their personal mnemonic ontology. Similarly, the Dominic System binds _31_ to the initials _CA_ , but the person _Carla Andrews_ in one mnemonist's system is _Charlie Aaron_ in another's, and the _characteristic action_ each person performs depends on the mnemonist's associations with that person. A mnemonic system, fully built out, is as personal as a writer's vocabulary — common in its grammar, deeply individual in its specific choices.

Why does this matter? Several implications.

First, _mnemonic technique cannot be transferred wholesale_. A novice who tries to adopt a memory champion's exact peg list will find it slower, less vivid, and more error-prone than the champion does — because the list relies on the champion's own associations, which the novice does not share. The novice's task is not to copy but to construct: take the principles, pick implementations that resonate with their own life, and build. This is one of the reasons mnemonic skill is hard to teach quickly. The principles can be taught in an afternoon; the implementation takes months of personal construction.

Second, _the personal nature of the system is part of why it works so durably_. A mnemonic system you have built for yourself, drawing on your own associations, is densely connected to the rest of your semantic network in ways that a borrowed system is not. Your peg word _moon_ (for _32_) might evoke a particular novel you read in college, or a song from your wedding, or a childhood story your mother told you. These idiosyncratic associations make _moon_ exceptionally memorable to you in a way that a standard reference list cannot capture. The personalization is not a quirk of the technique; it is part of why the technique succeeds.

Third, _mnemonic skill is, to a real extent, a craft of self-knowledge_. The good mnemonist knows which images work for them, which pegs feel sticky, which kinds of scenes their imagination produces vividly. They have invested time in noticing their own associative tendencies and building a system that exploits them. This is a kind of self-knowledge that the mnemonist's neighbor lacks not because the neighbor is less intelligent but because the neighbor has not done the work of self-mapping.

Fourth, and as a slight worry: this personal construction can become a constraint. A mnemonist who has invested years in a particular system may have difficulty switching, and their system can become a kind of cognitive lock-in. This is similar to language: the words you speak fluently now are the ones that come, not by choice but by the deep grooves of past use. Mnemonists, like speakers, are partly bound by their past work.

A pragmatic posture: treat mnemonic systems as _frameworks_ (universal, portable principles plus systematic structures) inside which you construct _implementations_ (your own peg words, your own person mappings, your own characteristic scenes). The framework can be borrowed; the implementation must be built. The person-action-object format used by current world memory champions is a borrowed framework; the specific persons, actions, and objects each champion uses is their own personal implementation, evolved over years.

This connects back, finally, to the book's larger question. _Memory_ is partly the brain (universal machinery) and partly the rememberer (idiosyncratic associations). Mnemonic technique sits at the interface. The brain is the same across users; the technique is the same across users; the implementation, layered on top, is personal. None of these layers alone is enough; all three are needed. This is the kind of claim the book has been building toward: memory is not purely a property of the brain, not purely a property of the rememberer, but a property of their interaction with the world via the techniques they use, the materials they encounter, and the lives they have lived.

**Q2.** The Major System trains a precise mapping from digits to consonant sounds, and through years of use this mapping becomes automatic. But the same brain that has built this mapping is also processing language constantly, in everyday speech, and there is no obvious way for the brain to know when to apply the Major-System interpretation and when to apply ordinary language. Yet practiced mnemonists report that the system does _not_ interfere with everyday speech — they don't accidentally hear the word _cat_ and think _7-1_ every time someone speaks. How might this be possible? What does the answer suggest about the architecture of cognitive control and the way mnemonic skills are integrated with the rest of cognition?

**Discussion:** This is one of the more subtle questions about mnemonic practice and connects to broader issues in cognitive control.

The empirical observation is correct: experienced mnemonists do not, in everyday speech, automatically transcode words back into digit sequences. The Major System mapping, while well-learned and fluent, does not "intrude" on ordinary language processing in the way a vivid memory or a strong association might. This is interesting because, naively, one might expect that a deeply learned mapping (digits ↔ consonants) would activate bidirectionally — encountering a _cat_ would trigger _7-1_ the way encountering _7-1_ triggers _cat_. It does not, in practice.

The probable explanation involves the role of _task context_ in cognitive control. The brain does not blindly run all overlearned associations; it runs them in context, and the context determines which mappings are active. When the mnemonist is in _memorization mode_ — explicitly trying to encode digits, with the Major System "loaded" as the active strategy — the digit-to-word mapping fires automatically. When the mnemonist is in _conversation mode_ , the same mappings are not loaded as the active strategy, and ordinary language processing dominates. The brain has machinery (largely prefrontal and executive) for selecting which cognitive strategies are active in a given context, and the Major System is one strategy among many, called up when needed and quiescent otherwise.

This is, on reflection, how _most_ skilled cognition works. A surgeon does not automatically translate every conversation into anatomical-cut planning; a chess master does not see every social situation as a chess position; a translator does not automatically translate every English sentence into French in their head, even though they could. Skilled cognitive systems are _context-bound_ : they activate when invoked and remain quiet otherwise. This is itself one of the most underappreciated facts about expertise. It is not the case that the expert is always seeing the world through their expertise; the expert sees the world through their expertise _when relevant_ and through ordinary cognition the rest of the time.

There is, however, a softer version of intrusion that mnemonists do report. Encountering a striking number in everyday life — a year, a phone number, a bill — sometimes triggers a quick "auto-decode" into peg-words even when the mnemonist had no plan to memorize the number. The reaction is something like the way a chess master sees a board configuration as a position even when not playing. The mapping is sufficiently deep that some material triggers it spontaneously. But this is far from systematic interference; it is a brief flicker, easily ignored.

What the answer suggests about cognitive architecture: mnemonic skills are _integrated_ with the rest of cognition through the same context-binding mechanisms that integrate any specialist skill. The Major System does not exist in a separate brain region from ordinary language; it uses the language-processing system in a special way under specific task conditions, and the conditions are gated by executive control. This is, conveniently, also why mnemonic skill does not require the practitioner to "switch off" their normal cognition — they can be a memorist and a normal conversationalist and a chess player and a parent, with each skill engaging when needed.

A deeper implication: skill acquisition is not just about adding capacities; it is about adding _selectively activated_ capacities that integrate with existing cognition without crowding it. The brain has solved a hard control problem: how to learn many specialized skills, hold them all simultaneously, and run only the one(s) currently relevant. This is why human cognition is so impressively flexible — and, by analogy, why a memory champion is not a kind of cognitive monoculture but a person with one specialized skill among many normal capacities. We will return to a related point in Chapter 8 when we discuss the limits of mnemonic skill: the memory champion, despite their virtuoso encoding, is not a different kind of thinker; they are an ordinary thinker with one extra trick. The trick is impressive; it is not transformative of cognition as a whole.

### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced _phonetic transcoding_ — the systematic conversion of digits into images — as the second pillar of the mnemonic tradition. Numbers are uniquely difficult for the human brain because the _exact number system_ (the one that handles precise digit strings) is symbol-bound and sparsely connected to the rest of cognition, while the _approximate number system_ (innate, evolutionarily ancient) handles only fuzzy magnitudes. The mnemonist transcodes digits out of the sparse number system and into the rich semantic-and-imagery systems via a phonetic code.

The _Major System_ maps each digit to a consonant sound; vowels and weak consonants are fillers; pairs of digits become words; words become images; images are placed in a Memory Palace. The system is not a magic memory enhancer; it is a _pre-processing pipeline_ that converts unfriendly material into friendly material before the encoding system handles it. Two competing peg systems — the _Dominic System_ (digits as people) and the _Number-Shape System_ (digits as shape-pictures) — illustrate that mnemonic technique is a design space rather than a single artifact, with elite memorists often constructing idiosyncratic blends.

Continuing Thread C: where Chapter 5's dialogue was _the ancients intuited spatial encoding; modern science confirmed it_ , this chapter's dialogue is _the ancients invented phonetic transcoding; modern science explains why it works on the brain we have_. Stanislas Dehaene's account of the dual number system provides the mechanism the practitioners had no way of naming. The next chapter examines _which_ images stick and which slide off — and turns the same insight onto a darker phenomenon: why hate ads, conspiracy imagery, and shock political content exploit the same affordances.

_Place the central idea of this chapter — that unfriendly material becomes memorable through phonetic transcoding into the rich systems of language, imagery, and space — in the study of your palace, on the desk. The study is the right room for transformation: a place where transcoding work happens._

## Chapter 7: Linking, Chunking, and the Power of Bizarre Imagery

Joshua Foer, an American journalist, spent a year training as a memory athlete in the early 2000s and eventually won the United States Memory Championship. In his book _Moonwalking with Einstein_ , he describes the mental world of competitive memorists. It is, he reports with mild embarrassment, _deeply strange_. To memorize a deck of cards in two minutes, a competitor walks a Memory Palace they have built and at each location places not a respectable image but a cartoonishly bizarre, often violent, often sexual, often absurd scene. A circus elephant balanced on a teacup. A celebrity strangling another celebrity. A grandmother committing acts the reader does not need described.

Foer was puzzled, at first. Why was the imagery so consistently this way? Why did every memorist's training, across every culture and every era of the mnemonic tradition, advise the same thing — _make the images bizarre, make them shocking, make them unforgettable_? It seemed like a quirky cultural inheritance, perhaps a Victorian holdover.

It is not. It is the most direct exploitation in the entire mnemonic toolkit of one of the most reliable findings in cognitive psychology: _distinctive material is dramatically more memorable than typical material_ , and the brain has dedicated machinery — emotion, attention, neuromodulation — for tagging the distinctive for preferential consolidation. When Cicero, in his treatises on rhetoric, advised orators to make their mnemonic images "active, sharply outlined, distinctive, and apt to encounter the spirit and to penetrate to its core," he was describing — without knowing it — what twentieth-century cognitive psychology would call the _von Restorff effect_ , what Allan Paivio would call _dual coding_ , and what neuroscience would later trace to the amygdala's role in tagging hippocampal traces for stronger consolidation. The mnemonic tradition's most peculiar piece of advice — _make it weird_ — turns out to be the most precisely targeted piece of advice in the entire tradition, exploiting brain machinery whose function is, in cognitive science's account, _exactly the function the mnemonists were exploiting_.

This chapter does four things. It introduces the von Restorff effect and explains why distinctiveness wins over repetition. It introduces Allan Paivio's dual-coding theory and explains why visual-plus-verbal encoding outperforms either alone. It traces the brain mechanism — the amygdala's emotional tagging of memory — that ties these two findings together into a single coherent picture. And it turns the same insight onto a darker question: hate ads, conspiracy imagery, and shock political content all exploit the same brain affordances that mnemonists exploit, and the mechanism that makes the Memory Palace effective is also the mechanism that makes manipulation effective. The chapter does not moralize, but it does not look away from the corollary either.

By the end of the chapter you will understand why your peg-word _rat_ must be doing something you would be embarrassed to describe at dinner — and why the political ad that haunted your sleep last week did so for exactly the same reason.

### 7.1 The Von Restorff Effect: Distinctiveness Wins

In 1933 a German psychiatrist named Hedwig von Restorff, working in Berlin, published a paper that was destined — though it would take some decades — to become a foundational finding of cognitive psychology. The setup was simple. She presented subjects with lists of items to memorize. The lists were structured so that one item in the list was _different_ from the others — a different category, a different format, a different visual presentation. For instance: ten three-letter syllables, with one digit triple in the middle; or a list of common nouns with one nonsense word in the middle.

The result, replicated many times since: _the different item is remembered far more reliably than the surrounding items_. This is the **von Restorff effect** , also called the _isolation effect_. Distinctiveness, in itself, drives memory. An item that stands out from its context — by category, by presentation, by emotional tone, by anything — is preferentially encoded and preferentially retrieved.

This is, when you think about it, a slightly strange finding. The distinctive item has not been studied longer; it has not been rehearsed more often; it does not have stronger semantic associations than its neighbors; it has no special importance to the subject. The only difference is that it is _different_. And that difference, by itself, increases its retention.

Why? Because the brain's encoding system is not a passive recorder. It is an _active selector_ , allocating consolidation resources to material flagged as more important — and one of the strongest signals of "this might be important" is _novelty in context_. A new sound in a familiar room captures attention; a new sentence in a familiar text captures attention; an item that does not fit the surrounding pattern captures attention. Attention drives encoding. Encoding drives consolidation. So distinctiveness drives retention, all the way down.

This is, in a sense, exactly what one would predict from a well-designed organism. Evolution did not build a brain to memorize uniformly; it built a brain to allocate cognitive resources where they were likely to matter. The new is more likely to matter than the familiar; the unexpected is more likely to matter than the expected. The von Restorff effect is the brain's encoding system reflecting this allocation rule. _Make the item different, and the system flags it for preferential treatment._

For the mnemonist, the implication is direct and powerful: _the more distinctive your imagery, the more memorable your encoding_. A bland image of a generic mat at the front door is well-formed but not distinctive — it could be any mat in any front door. A striking image of a rainbow-colored mat with a parrot perched on it screaming the word _Stop!_ is distinctive — there is no other image like it in your palace, and your encoding system will tag it accordingly. Bizarre imagery is not a quirk of mnemonic culture; it is precision targeting of the von Restorff effect.

#### Definition: The Von Restorff Effect

**The von Restorff effect** (also _isolation effect_) is the empirical finding that an item that is distinctive within its context — different in category, presentation, modality, emotional tone, or any salient property — is encoded more strongly and retrieved more reliably than items that fit the surrounding pattern. The effect is robust across many materials, paradigms, and ages, and is one of the most replicated findings in memory research.

In plain language, this means: _what stands out is what is remembered_. The brain treats distinctiveness as a signal of potential importance, and allocates encoding resources accordingly. The mnemonist who deliberately constructs distinctive imagery is exploiting this allocation rule directly; the advertiser who constructs a memorable jingle in a sea of forgettable jingles is doing the same; the comedian who lands a joke is doing the same; the political operative who designs a shocking image is doing the same.

#### Common Misconception

A reader sometimes assumes that the von Restorff effect predicts that _only_ the distinctive item is well remembered, and that _typical_ items in a list are essentially lost. This overshoots. The distinctive item is _more_ memorable than the typical items, often substantially. But the typical items are not at zero — their retention follows the curves we discussed in Chapter 4, modulated by the various features of memorability we have been cataloguing. The von Restorff effect is best thought of as a _boost_ to the distinctive item, not as a black hole that swallows the rest. In list-memorization tasks, the distinctive item often shows roughly twice the retention of typical items at the same delay; the typical items are not gone, just not as well-remembered. The effect is significant; it is not absolute.

### 7.2 Paivio's Dual Coding: Two Channels Beat One

In 1971, the Canadian psychologist Allan Paivio published _Imagery and Verbal Processes_ , a synthesis of two decades of his research that introduced what is now called **dual-coding theory**. The theory's central claim is simple: the mind has _two distinct cognitive channels_ for representing information — a verbal-linguistic channel that processes words and language, and a non-verbal imagistic channel that processes images, visual scenes, sounds, and other sensory representations. The two channels are _separable_ (they can each operate on their own) and _additive_ (when both are engaged simultaneously, the resulting trace is stronger than what either channel could produce alone).

Paivio's evidence came from many studies showing that material that could be both _named_ and _imagined_ — concrete words, objects, scenes — was remembered substantially better than material that could only be named (abstract words like _justice_ , _happiness_ , _integrity_) or material that was only an image (untitled photographs, abstract patterns). The combination of word-plus-image produced retention that exceeded the sum of either alone.

Why? Because each channel provides an independent route to retrieval. A memory encoded both verbally and imagistically can be reached via either route. If the verbal trace decays or is interfered with, the imagistic trace may still be intact, and vice versa. Two redundant routes are dramatically more robust than one route, because each compensates for the other's failure modes.

There is also, in modern accounts, a deeper computational story. The verbal and imagistic systems are anatomically distinct — broadly, language and imagery engage different cortical regions, with some shared substrate but substantial separation. When a representation is encoded in both, the trace is _spatially distributed_ across more brain real estate; the broader distribution means more redundancy and more cues for retrieval. A memory that lives only in verbal form is at the mercy of whatever happens to the verbal regions; a memory that lives in both has multiple homes.

The implication for mnemonic technique: _whenever possible, encode material both verbally and imagistically_. Saying the peg word _rat_ engages the verbal system; visualizing the rat clearly engages the imagistic system; doing both engages both systems and produces a substantially stronger trace than either alone. The Major System pipeline of Chapter 6 — digits → consonants → words → vivid imagery → palace placement — is by design a pipeline that ends in both channels simultaneously. The peg word is verbal; the scene is imagistic; together they exploit dual coding.

The implication generalizes far beyond mnemonics. It suggests that _any_ material learned with both verbal and imagistic engagement will be better retained than the same material learned in only one channel. A diagram alongside a textual explanation produces stronger learning than text alone; a teacher who combines spoken description with sketches on a board is exploiting dual coding; a learner who reads and then visualizes is doing better than a learner who only reads. The principle is sometimes called _the multimodal advantage_ and is one of the most robust findings in educational psychology.

#### Definition: Dual-Coding Theory

**Dual-coding theory** (Paivio, 1971 and subsequently) is the framework under which information can be cognitively represented in two distinct channels — a verbal-linguistic channel and a non-verbal imagistic channel — that are anatomically and functionally separable but additively contribute to memory. Material that engages both channels (e.g., a concrete word that names a vivid scene) is encoded more strongly than material that engages only one. The theory has been refined and contested in detail since 1971 but remains one of the most influential frameworks in the cognitive psychology of memory and learning.

In plain language: the mind has two notebooks — one for words, one for images. Material written in both notebooks survives better than material written in only one. Mnemonists, by deliberately constructing scenes for their peg words, are writing in both. Most everyday learners, who only read, are writing in only one — and are paying a memory cost for it.

#### Common Misconception

A common over-extension of dual-coding theory is the claim that "people are visual learners or verbal learners," and that lessons should be tailored accordingly. This is a misreading of the evidence. Dual-coding theory says that _all_ learners benefit, on average, from material that engages both channels — there is no robust evidence that some people benefit only from one and others only from the other. The "learning styles" framework, popular in education for some decades, has not held up well to rigorous scrutiny. What dual-coding theory actually licenses is the claim that _combined visual-and-verbal encoding generally outperforms single-channel encoding for most learners_ , which is a much weaker but much better-supported claim than "match the lesson to the learner's style." Mnemonists exploit this by combining verbal pegs with vivid imagery; teachers should exploit it by routinely combining spoken or written explanation with diagrams, examples, and spatial arrangements; learners should exploit it by reading and then visualizing what they have read. The principle is universal, not personalized.

### 7.3 Emotion: The Amygdala's Tag

The von Restorff effect tells us that distinctiveness drives memory. Dual-coding theory tells us that imagery-plus-language drives memory. A third major lever — closely related to but distinct from these — is _emotion_. Emotionally engaged material is encoded more strongly than emotionally neutral material. This is one of the most consistent findings in memory research, and it has a clear neural mechanism.

The mechanism centers on a small almond-shaped structure deep in the medial temporal lobe called the **amygdala** — situated, anatomically, very close to the hippocampus. The amygdala is the brain's emotional-tagging system. It receives inputs from many sensory pathways and from cognitive processing systems; it evaluates whether what is being processed is emotionally significant (threatening, rewarding, surprising, frightening, exciting, sexually charged); and when it detects emotional significance, it signals the rest of the brain — including the hippocampus — that this material deserves preferential encoding. The signal takes the form of neuromodulator release (notably norepinephrine and acetylcholine) that enhances synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus during the encoding of the emotionally tagged material.

The result, in everyday terms: emotionally charged events are remembered more vividly and more durably than emotionally neutral events. You remember the day you got engaged. You do not remember the morning of three Wednesdays ago. The amygdala tagged the engagement; it did not tag the Wednesday.

This is, mostly, an adaptive system. Material that is emotionally significant — frightening, threatening, rewarding, sexually salient — is more likely to be functionally important, and therefore more likely to deserve consolidation. The brain's emotional-tagging is evolution's solution to the allocation problem: how to know which of the millions of things that happen in a day deserve the consolidation budget. Emotion is the signal.

For the mnemonist, the implication is dramatic. _Emotionally charged imagery is encoded with substantially more vigor than emotionally neutral imagery._ A mat with a rat on it is bland — no amygdala tag, ordinary encoding. A mat with a rat on it that is _attacking your face_ , while you scream, is emotionally charged — amygdala fires, neuromodulator release, hippocampus encodes the scene with enhanced plasticity, the trace is laid down with substantially greater strength. The mnemonist's bizarre imagery — the violent, the sexual, the absurd, the shocking — is _exactly_ the imagery most likely to engage the amygdala and trigger the enhancement. The strangeness is not a quirk; it is a precision tool.

This is why memory champions, when they describe their mental palaces, sound disturbed. The Foer book is full of these descriptions, often with apologies. _I had to imagine the actor strangling the politician with a snake while a different politician watched approvingly._ The descriptions are uncomfortable to read because they are designed to be uncomfortable to imagine. The discomfort is the amygdala firing; the firing is the encoding enhancement; the enhancement is why the mnemonist can recall a deck of fifty-two cards in two minutes. The system rewards what is felt strongly. The mnemonist has learned to feel strongly on demand.

#### Definition: Amygdala Tagging

**Amygdala tagging** is the process by which the amygdala — a small structure in the medial temporal lobe specialized for emotional evaluation — flags emotionally significant material for preferential encoding by signaling the hippocampus and other memory structures, typically via neuromodulator release that enhances synaptic plasticity during encoding. Amygdala-tagged material is encoded more strongly and consolidated more durably than emotionally neutral material processed through the same channels. The tagging is largely automatic and does not require conscious decision; it depends on the amygdala's evaluation of incoming material against patterns of emotional significance built up over a lifetime.

In plain language: when something feels strongly, the brain flags it for stronger memory. The flag is biological — a literal release of neuromodulators that enhance the encoding machinery. Emotional engagement is not a metaphor for memory enhancement; it is the mechanism, named.

The three findings stack into a coherent picture. _Distinctiveness_ gets the encoding system's attention (von Restorff). _Dual coding_ spreads the trace across multiple brain systems (Paivio). _Emotional tagging_ triggers the neuromodulatory enhancement that strengthens the trace (amygdala). When all three are engaged together — a distinctive, vividly imagined, emotionally charged scene — the resulting trace is dramatically more durable than ordinary encoding. The mnemonic tradition has been exploiting all three together for 2,500 years, without naming any of them.

### 7.4 Linking and Chunking

Two more techniques deserve treatment in this chapter, because they are part of the standard mnemonic toolkit and because they exploit the same affordances we have been discussing.

#### Linking

The **linking** technique (also called the _story method_ or _chain method_) is a way of memorizing a sequence of items by constructing a linked chain of vivid images, each of which transitions naturally to the next. Where the Memory Palace anchors items to fixed locations, linking anchors them to _each other_ , with each item-image triggering the next-item-image through some visual or narrative connection.

To memorize the list _milk, eggs, bread, apples, broccoli_ , the linking method might construct: _a giant carton of milk overturns, spilling out a flood of cracked eggs, which roll across the floor and pile against a loaf of bread the size of a sofa, which in turn is being attacked by an army of apples that are biting their way through the crust, until the apples burst out the other side and reveal a tree of broccoli growing through the floor_. The reader recalls the list by following the narrative chain: milk → eggs → bread → apples → broccoli, each cued by the previous element's transition.

The linking method has advantages and disadvantages relative to the Memory Palace. _Advantages:_ it requires no pre-built spatial structure; you can construct a chain on the fly; the narrative engages the brain's story-processing machinery, which is highly developed. _Disadvantages:_ it is fragile — if you lose one link in the chain, you may lose everything that comes after it; reordering or random access (recalling the third item without traversing the first two) is difficult; the chain works for short sequences but becomes unwieldy beyond about ten items.
