NREM (especially slow-wave) sleep is most important for declarative memory; REM is most important for procedural skills, emotional memory processing, and creative integration.

The all-night cram is _anti-intellectual_ in a precise sense: by suppressing sleep, it disables the very consolidation machinery the day's encoding depends on. By contrast, the 90-minute afternoon nap completes a full sleep cycle and produces real consolidation — a sophisticated cognitive intervention for those whose schedules permit it.

Continuing Thread C, the chapter argued that the mnemonic tradition's vigil ethos has been structurally hostile to long-term retention. The integrated picture — encoding tools (Part II) + retrieval + spacing + sleep — is the full toolkit for durable memory practice; the mnemonic tradition over-invested in encoding, under-invested in retrieval and spacing, and actively worked against sleep. The next chapter will deliver the most disturbing finding in modern memory science: that retrieval is also re-encoding, and the memories you cherish most are partly your own composition.

_Place the central idea of this chapter — that sleep is the second half of learning, where the day's encodings are filed into durable cortical storage — in the bedroom of your palace, on the bed itself. The bedroom is the right room for sleep: a place where the work of the day continues into the night, in a register the awake mind cannot perform._
